transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-21
Start time (UTC): 16:00
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jonah Ruiz (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Head of ML, Aquifer), Tomas Alvarez (CTO, Aquifer), Nina Park (SRE, Aquifer)

Optional auto sections:
Summary: Quick scouting call to understand Aquifer's inference needs: long-context customer support transcripts (up to 200k tokens in session), multilingual (EN/ES/FR/JA), and the need to call internal tools (policy DB, ticketing). Exploring tradeoffs between Redwood hosted, dedicated, and private.
Topics: context length, model selection (open models), tool-calling, VPC/on-prem, security controls, cost/latency tradeoffs
Action items: see metadata above

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood inference, AE. Jonah, our SE, is on too. How are you folks doing?
[00:05] Priya: Hi Maya, thanks. Good. Excited to get into this — we got a lot to chew on.
[00:09] Tomas: Morning/afternoon. We'll try to keep this focused, we have some constraints around telemetry and on prem logs.
[00:14] Jonah: Great. Quick agenda— understand your workload shape, context lengths, language mix, tool-calling needs, and the security/infra constraints that push you toward hosted vs dedicated vs private.
[00:22] Nina: Also want to hear about latency for live support and costs — we have quite a few concurrent sessions.
[00:27] Maya: Cool. Priya, can you give a short description of the primary use case?
[00:31] Priya: Sure. We're building a virtual support assistant that ingests customer chat+voice transcripts and internal KBs. Typical session could be a 30-minute support conversation but we also want to keep a long history — sometimes threads reference conversations from months back. So effective context needs are... somewhere between 8k and up to maybe 150k tokens if we include embeddings + retrieved docs.
[00:46] Tomas: For regulatory reasons some logs have to stay inside our VPC for seven years. We also encrypt at rest with our HSM. So whatever you offer, needs to integrate with our KMS/HSM or be on-prem.
[00:56] Jonah: Understood. A couple clarifying q's — when you say 150k tokens, is that raw tokenized sequence or combined with retrieved passages? And are you thinking full autoregressive decoding across that entire window or a hybrid where you cache KV?
[01:05] Priya: Good question. It's a mix: we do long document retrieval and want the model to see a compacted context, but for certain root-cause investigations we want full context replay. So caching and prefix KV would be super helpful. We don't expect to run autoregressive over 150k tokens every call but need the option.
[01:18] Maya: That maps to some of our offerings. Hosted can support long context via model variants and smart retrieval but dedicated and private give more levers: custom KV cache sizing, larger sequence kernels, and model compilation tuned to your hardware.
[01:29] Nina: How much control does dedicated give us over quantization? We had bad hallucination when we tried 4-bit quantized variants internally.
[01:34] Jonah: Dedicated gives configuration profiles. You can pick quantization levels per model family and we provide recommended profiles for accuracy-sensitive vs cost-sensitive routes. We also run evals with your prompts to estimate quality impact. 4-bit is tricky for some families, especially if you need tool-calling reliability.
[01:47] Tomas: Tool-calling — we need the assistant to call our internal ticket API, plus a policy DB to check entitlements. So function calling is mandatory. Can Redwood route calls to internal endpoints when hosted?
[01:57] Maya: On hosted we support function/tool calling but for sensitive internal endpoints customers typically use a dedicated or private deployment so the network egress to internal APIs can stay private. We also support proxying via secure tunnels in dedicated setups.
[02:07] Priya: If we do hosted with a proxy, is the traffic still hitting your control plane? We need to make sure PII isn't stored in logs.
[02:13] Jonah: We can configure to not persist request bodies in logs; we also offer field-level redaction. For PII-sensitive work, the Private option keeps everything in your VPC and audit logs only.
[02:22] Maya: Quick aside — which open models are you evaluating? Have you run internal evals?
[02:26] Priya: We ran some initial tests on Llama 3 70B and Mistral Instruct 8x; multilang performance was okay but we saw latency spikes with long context. We're curious about models with native long-context vs retrieval augmented.
[02:36] Jonah: Right — model families differ: some have dedicated long-context architectures, others rely on chunking + retrieval. For example, we see different latency and RAM patterns for Llama derivatives versus purpose-built long-context models. Also, you mentioned Japanese — many open weights degrade in non-English unless fine-tuned.
[02:50] Tomas: Is Redwood doing quantized kernels per model? We maintain GPUs in-house for a POC and want to know how much tuning is required.
[02:56] Jonah: Our runtime selects kernels and compilation paths based on model arch and sequence lengths. For Dedicated, our team can run a kernel sweep on your reserved hardware to find the best mix. That reduces latency and allows more aggressive batching without breaking SLOs.
[03:09] Priya: Speaking of SLOs, our internal requirement is p95 < 400ms for one-shot replies on short queries, and under 2s for retrieval-augmented responses. For long-context investigative runs we can accept up to 6s.
[03:20] Maya: Those are helpful. Hosted can meet short-reply p95 for many models; dedicated will be more predictable for your high-concurrency user base. Private is the only way to fully control network egress and KMS.
[03:29] Nina: On the security side, we need SSO/SAML integration, RBAC, audit logs with immutable storage, and SOC2 compliance evidence. What's the difference vs hosted?
[03:37] Maya: Hosted supports SSO and RBAC, and we are SOC 2 Type II certified — we can send the report under an NDA. Dedicated adds dedicated tenancy and VPC peering options; Private gives you total control over identity and logging. We integrate with common KMS providers and HSMs via customer-managed keys.
[03:52] Tomas: How does cost scale for embedding storage and retrieval? We plan to store 20M doc vectors.
[03:58] Jonah: For very large vector stores, many customers use their own vector DB (we integrate via connectors) and cache hot vectors. Redwood Optimize helps recommend caching layers to reduce per-request embedding calls. We can run a projection on your QPS to estimate unit costs.
[04:13] Priya: Multilingual model selection — are there open models you'd recommend for EN/ES/FR/JA with acceptable latency?
[04:18] Jonah: There are tradeoffs: some models are stronger in multilingual NLU out of the box (some Mistral variants, Llama 3 finetuned multilingual), but you should run evals on your prompt set. We offer an eval harness to run A/B comparisons and measure hallucination rate and tool-calling fidelity.
[04:33] Maya: Important to note: for function calling reliability we typically avoid aggressive quantization. If tool-calls are critical, we recommend higher-precision variants for those routes.
[04:41] Nina: Can we mix routes? Like dedicated for high-throughput, hosted fallback for overflow?
[04:45] Maya: Yes — routing policies can split by latency requirement, cost, region, or token budget. You can route to hosted as a lower-cost fallback. We also have automated fallback to smaller/cheaper model variants if capacity is constrained.
[04:56] Tomas: We want to run a POC. Ideally: (1) host two models on a dedicated pool you provide for us to benchmark, (2) run sample prompts including tool calls and long-context replays, (3) measure latencies and tool call success. What's a realistic timeline?
[05:09] Jonah: We can spin up a dedicated pilot in ~2 weeks if you have a signed NDA and a short commitment. Pilot typically runs 2–4 weeks. We'll run the kernel sweep and do the prompt evals.
[05:18] Priya: Concerning telemetry — can we stream traces to our tracing system without exposing raw prompts?
[05:23] Jonah: Yes — we can send anonymized traces with token-level timing and cost, and optionally token deltas without content. Private deployments make that simplest, but dedicated can be configured too.
[05:33] Speaker 1: (mumble) sorry, quick question on billing — do you charge per-token on dedicated?
[05:36] Maya: On dedicated it's reserved capacity pricing (monthly commit) plus a small per-token to cover oversubscription; hosted is per-token. We'll include both examples in the pricing spreadsheet.
[05:45] Nina: Any limits on context length per call in hosted?
[05:48] Jonah: There are model-specific limits; we can support very long effective contexts via retrieval, KV caching, and snapshotting sessions. But for native 150k context windows you usually need dedicated or private plus a model that supports that long context.
[06:00] Tomas: What about data residency for EU users? We need region-specific hosting.
[06:04] Maya: We have regions in NA and EU and can pin workloads. Private deployments let you stay fully inside a customer's cloud region or on-prem.
[06:11] Priya: Can Redwood help with fine-tuning on our internal docs to improve Japanese?
[06:15] Jonah: Yes — we have model lifecycle tools for retraining/fine-tuning and versioning. For Private or Dedicated we can run fine-tuning jobs within your environment or on our infra with customer data controls.
[06:26] Maya: Quick demo idea — Jonah, can you show our eval harness and the prompt comparison sheet in the follow-up?
[06:30] Jonah: Yep we'll share a sandbox and a sample prompt harness. We'll run Llama 3 70B quantized vs Mistral longCxt variants and show tool-calling success rates.
[06:40] Priya: That'd be great. Also please include a sample of failure modes we saw — hallucination on policy checks.
[06:44] Maya: We'll do that. Any other blockers or exec stakeholders we should loop in?
[06:48] Tomas: CIO will want a short note on risk and cost — I'll loop them if we have a clear pilot scope. Also legal will need the SOC2 and data processing addendum.
[06:56] Maya: Noted. We'll send the security pack under NDA.
[07:00] Nina: Timeline — if we sign the NDA this week, when can pilot start?
[07:03] Maya: If NDA this week and pilot order approved, we can start provisioning next week and start tests in ~10 business days.
[07:11] Priya: Sounds good. Thanks.
[07:13] Maya: Thanks everyone. Recap: Maya to send pricing matrix and routing options; Jonah to send security pack and sandbox eval harness; Priya to share prompt set and latency targets.
[07:23] Tomas: Bye all.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcription quality: medium — some overlapping speech and a few proper nouns (model names and HSM vendor) may be slightly mis-transcribed.
